extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, USPTO examiners, policymakers, industry stakeholders (biotech, software), and public commenters on §101 subject-matter eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate and apply legal/regulatory standards and policy criteria for patent-eligible subject matter (biotech, diagnostics, computer-related inventions) across jurisdictions and in light of Supreme Court (Mayo/Alice/Myriad) jurisprudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic methods exclusion (with in vitro exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagnostic methods are not eligible. “Method of extracting samples and data from the human body, or methods of analyzing, e.g., comparing such samples and data with standards, by utilizing samples and data extracted from the human body […] preparatory treatment for measuring structures or functions of various organs of the human body” are not such diagnostic methods so long as they are not claimed in conjunction with diagnosing a disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some jurisdictions (e.g., JPO, KIPO, SIPO) carve out that methods consisting of steps separable from medical practice (e.g., treatment of samples extracted from the body or in vitro analysis) may be considered industrially applicable and not fall under the diagnostic-method exclusion. Example: EPO Technical Board found an in vitro method for diagnosing predisposition patent-eligible because technical steps were carried out in vitro and not directly on the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: In vitro/technical-steps criterion for diagnostics
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods that include steps performed outside the body (e.g., in vitro analysis of tissues or fluids taken from the human body) are not considered ineligible diagnostic methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in Japan and Korea; China allows methods to obtain information from a living human or to treat/test tissues/fluids provided they do not result in obtaining a diagnostic result. EPO case law treats steps of a 'technical nature' carried out in vitro as supporting eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural products / isolated biological material rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturally occurring products existing in their natural form generally are not patent eligible subject matter; however, biological material 'isolated from its natural environment or produced by means of a technical process' may be patented 'even if it previously occurred in nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EU Biotechnology Directive and EPC implementing rules implement this principle; several national guidelines (JPO, KIPO, SIPO) likewise allow patenting of artificially isolated natural substances. The isolated element may be patentable even if structurally identical to the in situ element.

rubrics_metrics.name: SIPO gene/DNA patentability conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A gene or a DNA fragment, and the process of obtaining it, can constitute patent eligible subject matter if: (1) it is isolated or extracted for the first time from nature; (2) the structure, morphology, or other physical/chemical parameters are unknown in the prior art; (3) it can be definitely characterized; and (4) it can be exploited industrially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SIPO examination guidelines articulate these four specific conditions as a checklist for determining patent eligibility of natural genetic material; applicants should show novelty of isolation, characterization, and industrial applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer program 'as such' exclusion (EPO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs for computers 'as such' are excluded from patent eligible subject matter under Article 52(2) and (3) EPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO case law: if the claimed invention causes a further technical effect beyond those effects which occur inevitably when any program is run (e.g., current flowing through circuitry), it is not considered a computer program 'as such.' Example: a program that brings about a technical effect beyond normal software/hardware interaction can be patent eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical-character / further-technical-effect test for software
rubrics_metrics.description: A computer-implemented invention is patent eligible if it brings about a 'technical effect' or 'technical solution' beyond the normal physical interactions between software and hardware.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by EPO and echoed in Federal Circuit focus on technological improvement; examples include software that controls a physical device or processes data in a way tied to physical/chemical relationships (e.g., gene-sequence-to-trait processing).

rubrics_metrics.name: China: exclusion of 'rules and methods for mental activities' and SIPO revision
rubrics_metrics.description: China Patent Act excludes 'rules and methods for mental activities'; however, SIPO revised guidelines state a claimed invention having technical characteristics will not be excluded from patentability because it contains a business method or rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-revision, SIPO treats business-method-containing claims as potentially patentable when technical characteristics are present. Practitioners should emphasize technical character in specifications and claims when pursuing business-method-related inventions in China.

rubrics_metrics.name: JPO hardware-implementation requirement for computer-related inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Under JPO guidelines, eligibility of computer-related technology turns on whether, when the invention is considered as a whole, its information-processing aspects are required to be 'specifically implemented by using hardware resources.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JPO provides non-exhaustive examples of patent-eligible computer-related inventions (e.g., software to control appliances, software tied to physical/chemical relationships); focus claims on concrete hardware implementation or specific machine execution to satisfy eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: KIPO software-plus-hardware / medium exception
rubrics_metrics.description: KIPO guidelines state that a computer program per se is not a statutory invention, but software claimed in conjunction with hardware, the operating method of the combination, and a computer-readable medium containing the software that implicates the combination is patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims that recite a specific machine, combination, or computer-readable medium with functional tie-ins to hardware to avoid 'program per se' rejections in Korea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo/Alice two-step patent-eligibility framework (as-applied standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supreme Court's two-part eligibility test established in Mayo and developed in Alice (commonly applied in U.S. practice): (1) determine whether the claim is directed to a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., law of nature, natural phenomenon, abstract idea); (2) if so, determine whether claim elements, considered individually and as an ordered combination, contain an 'inventive concept' that transforms the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framework is the focal point of U.S. eligibility analysis and litigation; commentators debate its scope and application. Practical guidance: draft claims and specifications to recite concrete implementations, inventive concept details, and technical improvements to survive each step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to claim a specific way, not just a result (anti-preemption principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents should be awarded for the particular way an inventor achieved a result rather than claiming only the result itself; claiming only the abstract result can preempt others from achieving the same utility by different means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize specific algorithms, mechanisms, technical steps, or implementations in claims and disclosures; avoid claiming only the problem and its abstract solution. This principle is frequently invoked in software and business-method contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption concern in §101 analysis (and controversy over its use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility analysis often considers whether a claim would 'preempt' use of a fundamental building block (abstract idea, law of nature), but critics argue that this imports novelty/obviousness considerations from §§102/103 and conflates separate patentability doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to explain how claimed subject matter does not preempt all practical applications of a basic concept by reciting limiting inventive features; note that reliance on preemption is controversial and may be viewed as overlapping with other statutory requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for 'technical improvement' / 'technological solution' as entitlement to eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A focus on whether the invention provides a technological improvement or technological solution can be central to eligibility determinations (emphasized in Federal Circuit precedent and many commentator submissions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft and argue claims to show measurable technological benefits or specific technical effects (e.g., improved processing, reduced resource usage, improved device performance) rather than abstract advantages or business benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy/evidentiary use of §101 to police low-quality/overly-broad patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Many stakeholders view §101 as a tool for weeding out vague, low-quality, or overly-broad patents—particularly in software and business-method domains—and as a cost-saving defense in litigation (e.g., early motion to dismiss).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect §101 challenges to be used as an early-stage litigation tactic; applicants seeking robust portfolios should provide detailed disclosure of inventive concepts and implementation specifics to reduce vulnerability to eligibility-based attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand for objective, predictable, administrable eligibility criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics argue the Mayo/Alice two-step test is 'hopelessly subjective and unworkable' because key terms like 'abstract' and 'substantially more' lack objective definitions; calls exist for transparent, objective, predictable, and simple rules defining eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting or prosecuting, articulate clear factual support for why claims are concrete/technical and explain application of precedent; policymakers/examiners are urged to develop clearer bright-line or technology-specific guidance to improve predictability.
